content: To ensure the quality of HIV testing services, it is essential to monitor various performance indicators regularly. These include turnaround times for individual assays and overall testing reports, rates of discrepant or invalid results, specimen rejection rates, stock-outs of test kits and supplies, and the frequency of test kit expiration. Such monitoring helps identify non-conformance and areas requiring improvement. Testing services must conduct both internal and external quality assessments. Internal assessments often involve audits performed by site supervisors or district health management teams. These audits should ideally occur every three to six months and involve observing testing practices. In some cases, internal audits may be conducted by staff members who are not directly involved in the task but are familiar with the process. This approach aligns with quality activities like supportive supervision and ongoing staff mentoring. Observing testing procedures during assessments can help prioritize areas for improvement. Participation in external quality assessment (EQA) programs is crucial where available. EQA provides assurance to clients that assays are performed accurately, results are reproducible, and errors are identified and corrected. EQA typically involves proficiency testing schemes, which include follow-up actions for unacceptable results to implement corrective measures. Retesting is recommended for all individuals newly diagnosed as HIV-positive, particularly before initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART). This ensures the accuracy of the diagnosis. Retesting should not rely on dried blood spot (DBS) specimens as an EQA mechanism, especially given the recommendation to retest all seropositive individuals prior to ART initiation. Testing services must identify areas requiring improvement, plan and implement changes, and evaluate their impact. Improvements can occur at the site, district, or national levels, depending on the issue. Local factors, such as adjusting opening hours or client flow, may define site-level improvements. Data from internal audits, EQA participation, and on-site supportive supervision can guide process enhancements. Corrective actions address problems by eliminating root causes or reducing recurrence, while preventive actions aim to avoid potential issues. Client satisfaction is a critical component of quality assurance. This includes meeting the expectations of both internal clients (e.g., healthcare workers) and external clients (e.g., individuals undergoing testing). Delivering accurate results promptly is paramount. Training and sensitizing the health workforce can improve inclusivity and attitudes toward key populations. Privacy and confidentiality must be maintained within testing facilities, including separate waiting areas for additional testing. Testing facilities should be clean, comfortable, and well-lit, with adequate ventilation and waste disposal systems. The ambient temperature should align with assay manufacturer recommendations, and climate-controlled areas are preferred. Universal precautions must be observed, assuming all specimens are potentially infectious. Staff should be trained in biological and chemical safety measures, and one staff member at each site should act as a safety focal point. For HIV testing conducted outside facilities, providers must ensure safety for both themselves and clients. This includes observing universal precautions, proper waste disposal, and protecting client confidentiality and privacy. Quality assurance is an ongoing process. Providers and managers must continuously monitor and evaluate their programs to improve service quality. A functioning quality management system requires the involvement of all stakeholders at national, subnational, facility, and community levels. Various quality improvement methods have been applied in healthcare, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, over the past two decades. The choice of method depends on the country context, policy-maker commitment, and the complexity of the issues to be addressed. The World Health Organization (WHO) supports the implementation of high-quality HIV services and provides guidance on selecting appropriate quality measures.
